rows.title: Dry tide chalked early
rows.summary: The reeve's clerk has moved today's dry tide two hours earlier than yesterday's mark. Wulfstan saw water in the far channels at dawn, hours early; Jessop chalked the new mark after visiting the reeve's house.

rows.title: Cart tracks to the lower district
rows.summary: Fresh hand-cart ruts cross the deep channel and run toward the drowned rows of the lower district, between two roofs like a gate.

rows.title: Tam trapped under the fish market
rows.summary: Tam Kemp is pinned under his cart in a hole in the fish market floor while seep water rises around him.

rows.title: The hiss on the flats
rows.summary: A low steady hiss, like a distant kettle, is coming from out past the rows: the water returning early.

rows.title: The sea returns
rows.summary: For the first time since the Leaving, the sea is coming back across the outer flats, less than an hour away and higher than the rows' first floors.

rows.title: The sea floods the rows
rows.summary: The returning sea has drowned the north rows to the eaves; only roofs, chimneys and lamp poles stand above it.

rows.title: The customs bell rehung
rows.summary: The customs bell hangs in its frame in the tower again, raised on a rope through the hook and a stone bollard capstan.

rows.title: The customs bell rings
rows.summary: The customs bell rang from the tower over the returned sea; Saltmarrow's temple bell answered and lanterns moved along the harbour wall.

rows.title: A skiff from Saltmarrow
rows.summary: A harbour skiff with two rowers and Hereward Jessop in the stern is rowing from Saltmarrow to the customs tower.

rows.title: Hereward's confession
rows.summary: On the harbour wall Hereward Jessop told Saltmarrow the reeve had hidden Mara Tarrow in the customs tower for six years and suppressed her warnings of the sea's return.

rows.title: The wall turns on the reeve
rows.summary: After Mara wrote her testimony on the tally board, the whole harbour wall took up the runners' whistle against Reeve Baldwin Thorne.

rows.title: The last lamp
rows.summary: Isk lit the Lantern Wives' lamp one last time, for nobody lost, after Mara took down her own red cloth.

rows.title: The first high water rung
rows.summary: Isk and Mara rang the first true high water from the customs tower; Saltmarrow answered with lanterns, and Mara spoke again.

known/known: Isk grew up in Saltmarrow, the harbour town the sea abandoned forty years ago. She runs the exposed flats at dry tide, pulling salvage out of the drowned lower district before the water comes back for a few hours each night. Her mother went out on the flats six years ago and never came back; the salvage guild wrote her down as lost and kept her share. Isk owes the guild's tallyman for a winter of credit and carries her mother's brass tide-reckoner, which has never kept true time.
Opening scene: the model introduced the initial situation before the player acted.

Morning in Saltmarrow [[L1]] smells of dried weed and lamp smoke. From the old harbour wall you can see what the sea left behind forty years ago: a grey plain of mud running out to the horizon, ribbed with channels, and the roofs of the lower district standing up out of it like teeth. Mooring rings hang on the wall above your head, rusted open, waiting for boats that stopped coming before you were born.

A crowd of runners has already gathered at the guild's tally board, where a clerk in an ink-stained apron is nailing up the day's contracts. One sheet is pinned higher than the rest and carries the guild's red thumbprint: the bell of the old customs house, wanted whole, paid in coin rather than credit. Two runners read it, laugh, and walk away. The customs house sits furthest out on the flats.

Below the board, Hereward Jessop [[B]], the reeve's tide clerk, a thin man with a slate and a satchel of chalk, is redrawing the tide marks on the wall. Yesterday's dry tide is still there, ghosted under his new line, and the two do not agree. He has moved the opening two hours earlier and keeps glancing at the sky as if it might argue.

At the chandlery door behind you, a woman is hanging bundles of tallow candles from a pole. She is Philippa Kemp [[A]], and she sells lamp oil to every runner who goes out. Today she is not calling her prices. She is studying the faces coming off the stairs from the flats, one by one, and when yours comes level with her she steps into your way.

"You run the flats," she says. "My nephew Tam went out at the last dry tide with a hand cart. Did you see a boy with a hand cart?"

Philippa Kemp's nephew Tam went out on the flats at the last dry tide with a hand cart and has not come back.
The guild posted a coin-paid contract for the bell of the old customs house, furthest out on the flats.
"No boy with a cart, not on my stretch," I tell Philippa. "Which channel did Tam take, and when did he leave?"

Philippa Kemp [[A]] hears "no" and nothing after it. Her eyes have already left you for the stairs, where two more runners are coming up with mud to the knee and sacks over their shoulders.

"Then you were looking at your own feet," she says, not unkindly, just tired. "Everyone who goes out says the same. Not my stretch. Not my channel." She ties off the last bundle of candles with a jerk that nearly snaps the string. "If I knew which channel he took, I'd not be standing here asking strangers."

She steps past you to the next runner, a broad man with a split lip, and asks him the same question in the same words. He shakes his head before she has finished.

Along the wall, Wulfstan [[C]] the weaver has come out of his doorway to watch, a skein of grey wool looped over one arm. He catches your eye, glances at Philippa's back, and gives the smallest shrug, as if to say she has been at this since dawn. Then he goes back inside.

Below the tally board, Hereward Jessop [[B]] finishes his new chalk line and steps back to look at it. The two tide marks sit one above the other on the wall, two hours apart, and he does not rub out the old one.

I cross to the tide clerk at the wall. "Dry feet. Why'd you move the dry tide two hours early?"

You cross the few yards of wet flagstone to the wall. Hereward Jessop [[B]] hears the greeting and does not give the answer to it. He blows chalk dust off his slate, writes something small in the corner, and keeps his back to you as if the wall were the only thing on the harbour that could talk.

The new mark is fresh and square. The old one under it is smudged where someone has already tried to rub it out with a thumb and given up.

It is Wulfstan [[C]] who answers, from his doorway two houses along. He has come back out with the grey skein and is winding it onto his fist as he talks.

"He won't tell you," he says. "Asked him myself at first light. Reeve's orders, that's all he'll say, and he's said it to every runner on the wall." He tips his head toward the mud. "But I'll tell you what I saw from my window at dawn. The water was in the far channels already. Hours before it should have been. Then it went out again like it had forgotten something."

He snaps the wool off short with his teeth.

"Jessop chalked it after he came back from the reeve's house. Not before."

I flip open my mother's tide-reckoner, set it against the two chalk marks, and use Tidecount to feel for how long until the water comes back.

The tide-reckoner [[I4]] opens with a click that is louder than it should be. Its brass face is scratched with channel names in your mother's small hand, and the needle settles, shivers, and settles again. You hold it up beside the chalk until both marks sit behind the glass.

Then you stop looking and let Tidecount do the reading. It comes the way it always comes, as a slow pressure along the jaw, like biting down on something cold. The flats are empty now; you can feel that much as plainly as the stone under your boots. But the water is not far. It is sitting out past the furthest channels, close, and it is coming back in a little under four hours. Not at the old mark. Not at Jessop's new one either. Sooner than both.

And it is not coming evenly. The far channels fill first, out where the customs house stands, then the water runs back toward the wall along the deep cuts. Anyone working the far district would have the least time of all.

Hereward Jessop [[B]] has turned around. He looks at the open reckoner in your hand the way people look at a fortune-teller's cards.

"Put that away," he says. "The reeve's mark is the mark. If you want to go out on a guess, go out on a guess, but don't stand at my wall reading that old clock at people."

I go to the tally board and ask the guild clerk what the customs-house bell pays, and whether I can sign for it.

You walk the length of the wall to the tally board. The guild clerk in the ink-stained apron is gone; the shutter of the tally house beside the board is half down, and a hand bell sits on the sill for anyone who wants to wake whoever is inside.

The customs-house sheet is still pinned high, above the rest. Up close you can read it: one bronze bell, the old harbour bell from the customs house tower, to be brought to the tally house whole and uncracked. Thirty coin on delivery. Under the sum, in a different ink, someone has added: no advance, no credit, no claims for lost carts.

Hereward Jessop [[B]] has followed you along the wall with his chalk satchel, on his way somewhere else. He stops long enough to tap the sheet with his slate.

"You sign at the window," he says. "Ring and wait. They'll put your name in the book and your name on the bell, and if you come back without it, your name stays in the book." He looks at the far flats, then at you. "Thirty coin is what they pay when nobody local will go. Philippa Kemp [[A]] Ask yourself why the out-of-towners laughed."

He walks on toward the reeve's end of the harbour without waiting for an answer.

I ring the hand bell on the sill and wait at the window to sign for the bell.

The hand bell is cracked, and it makes a flat clank instead of a ring. You give it two, and then you wait.

Inside the tally house [[L2]] something scrapes across a floor. The shutter goes up the rest of the way with a bang, and a woman leans her elbows on the sill: the clerk from the board, ink still on her apron, now with a pen behind each ear. Close up she is older than she looked at a distance, grey at the temples, with the flat patience of someone who has watched a lot of runners go out.

She follows your eyes to the high sheet on the board and does not need telling which contract.

"The customs bell," she says. She pulls a long ledger out from under the counter and lets it fall open on the sill. Most of the page is names with lines through them. "Una Rendle. I keep the book. Name goes here, mark goes here. The bell comes back whole or it doesn't come back. Lose a cart, lose a rope, that's your loss, not the guild's."

She uncaps the ink, turns the ledger to face you, and holds out the pen.

I take the pen and write my name in the book: Isk Tarrow. "Has anyone else signed for the customs bell before me?"

The pen is cheap and scratchy, and the ink is thinned with something that smells of vinegar. You write your name under the last line, Isk Tarrow, and the letters sit wet and dark at the bottom of a page full of crossings-out.

Una Rendle [[D]] turns the ledger back toward herself, reads your name, and blots it with the side of her hand.

"Before you?" She runs a finger up the page without looking at it. She knows where it goes. "Two this month. A pair of brothers off the coast road, signed together. One came back without the bell and without his brother." The finger stops on a double line. "Crossed out the both of them."

She turns back one page.

"And yesterday a boy put his name down for it. Tam Kemp. Wrote it big, like he was proud of it." She taps a name that has no line through it. "Not crossed out. Book says he's still out there, and the book only knows what people come back and tell it."

She closes the ledger on your wet name and looks at you over it.

"Dry tide's on the reeve's mark. Bell's in the tower, if the tower's still standing. Bring it back whole."

Philippa Kemp's General Store is entered from Saltmarrow; the journey ends there.
I go back along the wall into Philippa's chandlery. "Tam signed for the customs bell yesterday. That's where he went." Then I ask her for a coil of rope and what it costs.

You leave the tally window and walk back along the wall, past Wulfstan [[C]]'s shut door, to the chandlery. Over its lintel someone has painted Philippa Kemp [[A]]'s General Store, but nobody on the wall has ever called it anything but the chandlery. Inside it is dim and close, hung with candles, coiled line, tins of pitch and lamp wicks bundled like straw. Philippa Kemp [[A]] is behind the counter, cutting wick with a knife too big for the job.

She looks up when you come in, already shaking her head, ready to hear another no.

Then she hears what you actually said. The knife stops. For a moment she just looks at you, and her face does something complicated, relief and fright arriving at the same time and neither one winning.

"That stupid boy. That stupid, stupid boy." She puts the knife down very carefully, as if she does not trust her hands with it. "He said he'd find a job that paid in coin. I thought he meant carting for the guild." She wipes her face with the back of her wrist. "The customs house. Nobody goes that far out."

You ask about the rope, and she reaches up without looking and pulls down a coil of tarred hemp, thirty feet, and drops it on the counter between you.

"Four coin, on any other day." She keeps her hand on it. "Three for you, if you're going out where he went. And if you see him, you tell him his aunt will skin him."

I put three coin on the counter for the rope. "I'll tell him. Then I'll bring him back so you can do it yourself."

You count three coins out of your purse and set them on the counter, one at a time, beside the rope. They are old copper, green at the edges.

Philippa Kemp [[A]] sweeps them into her palm without counting them again and slides the coil across to you. The tar on it is fresh enough to come off on your fingers.

Went out to the customs tower each month at dry tide with a basket, carrying Mara Tarrow's tide figures back to the reeve. rows.name: Jocosa Kettle
rows.summary: A salvager who runs the north rows of the drowned district; carries a long ash hook-pole and an oilskin hat. Ran the drowned rows with Isk's mother Mara Tarrow for nine years. Was the last person to see Mara Tarrow, going in between the two roofs under the Lantern Wives' lamp. Has a floating door she poles like a barge with her hook-pole. rows.summary: Philippa Kemp's nephew; fell through the fish market floor with his hand cart and is pinned under it. Hurt his left shin; lost his hand cart in the flooded hole under the fish market. rows.name: Isk Tarrow
rows.title: Flat-runner
rows.backstory: Isk grew up in Saltmarrow, the harbour town the sea abandoned forty years ago. She runs the exposed flats at dry tide, pulling salvage out of the drowned lower district before the water comes back for a few hours each night. Her mother went out on the flats six years ago and never came back; the salvage guild wrote her down as lost and kept her share. Isk owes the guild's tallyman for a winter of credit and carries her mother's brass tide-reckoner, which has never kept true time.

rows.rule: The rank ladder is F,E,D,C,B,A,S,SS,SSS, from lowest to highest: F, E, D, C, B, A, S, SS, SSS. Each step up is clearly stronger than the one below it. Anyone on a higher rung than the player is stronger than the player. There are no rungs beyond these nine.

The economy is scarce coin, salvage as currency. Scarce coin: minted coin is rare, hoarded, and a price in coin always stings. Salvage as currency: brass fittings, rope, nails, glass and drowned cargo pass hand to hand in place of coin, valued by weight and by the guild's tally board.

Hooks come as debts, salvage contracts, the missing. Debts: someone is owed, and the owing pulls people into errands. Salvage contracts: paid, dated jobs to bring something specific back off the flats. The missing: people lost on the flats or in town, and those still looking for them.

rows.choice: the salvage guild and the harbour reeve
rows.rule: Ordinary life is squeezed by the salvage guild and the harbour reeve. The salvage guild: keeps the tally of every runner's take and debt, sets salvage prices, and writes the lost off its books. The harbour reeve: the town's law, taxes the dry harbour, and decides who may go out on the flats and when.
Under relative ranks, NPC ranks are set against the player's own rank. Most people sit near the player; a few veterans sit a rung or two above, and a higher rung is stronger.
Under some trained NPCs, a few people have a ranked skill that matches their trade. Most townsfolk have none worth ranking.
Under moderate density, a scene holds a handful of people: one or two to talk to and a few more passing through.
Under normal difficulty, enemies usually sit at the player's rank, sometimes one rung above, and rarely more.
Loot is mundane common. Mundane common: useful ordinary goods turn up often; rare goods are uncommon finds; enchanted goods are almost never found.

Magic is rare and uncanny. Rare: most people never see true magic, and many doubt it exists. Uncanny: when it shows, it feels wrong and unexplained, and a public spell draws fear, gossip and the reeve's attention.
Under lasting injuries, a lost fight leaves the player hurt in ways that linger: wounds, limps and scars that take days to mend. Death comes from repeated or reckless harm, not one bad fall.
Under balanced detail, a scene gives enough sensory grounding to place the player, then moves to what people do and say. It avoids both bare summaries and long description.
Under the standard learning rule, a new skill is earned by practice, by teaching, or by surviving something that demanded it.

The tone is salt-worn, quiet dread, small kindnesses. Salt-worn: everything is weathered, patched and tired, people and buildings alike. Quiet dread: the threat is felt more than seen, in the tide, the debts and the missing. Small kindnesses: people still share bread, warnings and a hand up, and those moments matter.

Tech is late medieval. Late medieval: iron tools, block and tackle, lanterns, clockwork in rich houses, hand pumps and printed notices exist; gunpowder is rare and costly; there are no engines, steam or electric light.
Under normal check difficulty, a reasonable act by a capable person usually succeeds. Hard or rushed acts fail often.
The subtle blue-window system is a faint pane at the edge of sight that only the player sees. A notice may reveal a gained level, a new skill or a rank, in one short line.
Leveling is on. The player gains XP for meaningful acts and rises in levels over time.
The game system is off. No status window, quest note, achievement or system prompt appears in the story.
Proficiencies are on. Specialized acts such as salvage, tide-reading, surgery or lockwork go best with a learned proficiency.
Dice checks are on. Speech, strength, lore, events and encounters are settled by a roll against the act's difficulty, and the result stands.
Under normal frequency, an event check comes when time passes or the scene turns, not on every action.
Under normal frequency, an encounter check is called when the player travels, waits in the open, or enters a risky place.
Under normal frequency, an entirely new skill is discovered now and then, after real practice or a lesson, not every day.
Under learned access, the player may try a specialized act without its proficiency, but it is unreliable until the proficiency is learned from practice or a teacher.
The peoples are human. Human: the only people common in this world; everyone met is human unless the story shows otherwise.

rows.summary: Morning in Saltmarrow [[L1]]: a guild contract for the customs-house bell paid in coin, the reeve's clerk chalking the dry tide two hours early, and the chandler Philippa Kemp [[A]] asking after her missing nephew Tam.
Isk told Philippa Kemp [[A]] she had not seen Tam and asked which channel he took; Philippa, worn out from asking, brushed her off without an answer.

Isk asked the tide clerk Hereward Jessop [[B]] why the dry tide moved; he ignored her. The weaver Wulfstan [[C]] said Jessop only cites reeve's orders, and that he saw water in the far channels at dawn, hours early, before it drew out again.

Isk used Tidecount with her mother's tide-reckoner: the water will return in a little under four hours, sooner than either chalk mark, filling the far channels by the customs house first. Hereward Jessop [[B]] told her to put it away.

Isk read the customs-house contract: one bronze bell brought whole to the tally house, thirty coin on delivery, no advance. The guild clerk was inside; Hereward Jessop [[B]] said she signs at the tally-house window and warned that the pay is what they offer when no local will go.
At the tally-house window the guild clerk Una Rendle opened the contract ledger for the customs bell, set out the terms, and offered the pen.

Isk signed for the customs-house bell in Una Rendle [[D]]'s ledger. Una said two brothers signed this month and one never came back, and that Tam Kemp signed for the same bell yesterday and is not crossed out: the book has him still out on the flats.

Isk went into Philippa Kemp [[A]]'s chandlery and told her Tam signed for the customs-house bell. Philippa, shaken, said nobody goes that far out. She offered a thirty-foot coil of tarred rope for three coin instead of four, since Isk is going where Tam went.
Isk paid Philippa three coin for a thirty-foot coil of tarred rope. Philippa refused to take Isk's promise to bring Tam back, saying too many runners have promised that before.
Isk bought a thirty-foot coil of tarred rope from Philippa Kemp [[A]] for three coin, and Philippa showed her how to carry it over the shoulder so it comes free with one pull.

Isk left the chandlery, went down the harbour stairs onto the flats, and set out along the deep channel toward the customs house tower. The water in the channel bottom is cold and flowing slightly outward.

Isk found fresh hand-cart ruts crossing the deep channel [[L4]]; they turn away from the customs house toward the drowned rows of the lower district, with one small worn boot print where the cart bogged.

Isk tried to climb the steep right bank of the deep channel [[L4]]; the lip gave way, she slid back and wrenched her right elbow. The cart ruts climb out a few yards further on, where the bank is lower.

Isk tried the broken-down ramp where the cart left the channel; her left leg sank into soft mud to the knee and the knee wrenched as she fell. She is still below the lip of the bank. In the rut she saw a small spread handprint where someone else fell.

The sky clouded over. Isk crawled up the cart ramp on her belly and got her shoulders over the lip before the last handhold of crust sheared off; she slid back down two body lengths, unhurt but still below the bank.

Isk limped along the channel to a low hard stretch of bank at a bend, got half over it, and wrenched her side when her bad knee would not follow; she slid back into the channel. From there she can see an unlit lamp on a pole between the two roofs the cart ruts head for.

Isk used Tidecount sitting in the deep channel [[L4]]: the water returns in a little over two hours, far channels first, and the deep channel [[L4]] is one of the cuts it runs home along, so it will be among the first places on this side to fill. Someone out of sight is whistling a runner's two-note call.
Isk whistled and shouted for help; the salvager Jocosa Kettle, who runs the north rows, came to the bank and lowered her hook-pole for Isk to hold while she walks up.

Jocosa Kettle [[F]] hauled Isk up the bank with her hook-pole. Hearing Isk's name, she said she ran the rows with Isk's mother Mara for nine years. She saw Tam Kemp take his hand cart into the drowned rows past the Lantern Wives' lamp yesterday, and warned that the rows are a maze and no road to the customs house.

Jocosa Kettle [[F]] agreed to walk Isk to the Lantern Wives' lamp and through the first two rows of the drowned district, no further, because she has salvage waiting; she told Isk to step only where she steps, and set off toward the roofs.

Isk followed Jocosa Kettle [[F]] across the hard mud, stepping in her prints, to the two drowned rooftops; Jocosa was curt and quiet. Between the gables hangs Nearby street, an old ship's lantern smoked black, with a faded red cloth tied under it.

Under the Lantern Wives' lamp Jocosa explained that a red cloth marks where a runner was last seen and never found. This lamp was hung for Isk's mother: Jocosa saw Mara go in between these two roofs six years ago, the night the water came back early.

Isk followed Jocosa between the two roofs into the first row of the drowned district, a half-buried street. At the first corner the cart ruts bend right toward the old fish market, where the floor is rotten; Jocosa's way lies left to the second row.

Isk thanked Jocosa and told her to get her pipe before the water does; it reminded Jocosa of Isk's mother and she left angry for the second row. Isk followed the cart ruts right to the old fish market, a long covered hall with half its roof tiles gone; the ruts go in under the eaves, and something inside is dripping.

Inside the old fish market [[L7]] Isk found a cart-shaped hole in the rotten plank floor. Tam Kemp answered from inside it: he fell through with his cart, his leg is pinned under it, and seep water is rising up out of the ground below, already at his chest.

Isk tied the tarred rope to a stone counter leg, spread herself flat on the rotten planks, and fed the rope down to Tam, pinned under his cart in the flooding hole. Panicking, he grabbed it badly and pulled, and the board under Isk cracked.

Isk talked Tam into tying the rope under his arms and pulled while he pushed off his cart; the cart rolled and Tam came out of the flooding hole. Both lie flat on the fish market planks; Tam's left shin is badly bruised, and the cart sank.

Isk untied the rope and crawled with Tam along the planks out of the fish market to the doorway. Outside, Tam refused to leave without his dead uncle's hand cart, which sank in the hole with a bell-rope clapper fitting he says he found in the rows off the customs house.

Tam reluctantly agreed to leave the cart. Isk spotted a drowned house four doors down whose collapsed front wall makes a rubble ramp up to a low tiled roof with a broad chimney stack. The air turned hot and hazy, and a distant steady hiss is coming from out past the rows.

Isk got Tam up the rubble slope four doors from the fish market onto a low tiled roof and sat him against the chimney stack; she tied the rope round the chimney. Tam is sullen and silent. From the roof a thin white line shows along the whole horizon, and the hiss is louder.

On the chimney roof [[L8]] Isk used Tidecount on the white line: it is the sea itself returning across the outer flats for the first time in forty years, less than an hour away, higher than the rows' first floors. Her mother's reckoner needle is spinning. Tam asked if it is the tide.

Isk tied Tam fast to the chimney with the rope, but the wet tarred line ran out before it would go round her too; she is holding a loop of it wound round her fist. The distant hiss has become a roar, and the roof tiles are humming.

The sea came down the rows as a man-high wall of water, swallowed the rubble slope and the streets, and left the chimney roof [[L8]] a hand's width above a moving brown sea. Isk held on by the rope loop and the chimney; Tam, roped on, came through coughing. Isk's hand is torn by the rope, and the water is still rising slowly.

While Isk and Tam waited on the chimney roof [[L8]] the water rose tile by tile; a floating door knocked the roof, Isk's feet went out on the wet tiles and she slid down to the waterline, held only by the rope loop round her fist. Tam is hauling uselessly on the rope above her.

Too exhausted to climb, Isk failed to go up the rope; her grip opened, she dropped back to the rope's end and badly wrenched her side again. Tam braced against the chimney and held the rope but cannot lift her. She hangs waist-deep at the waterline.

Isk whistled and shouted for Jocosa; Tam joined in. Jocosa answered and came poling a floating door across the flooded street with her hook-pole. She hooked Isk by the collar and, with Tam pulling on the rope, dragged her out of the water onto the door.

A sea storm broke over the flooded rows. Jocosa said the door will barely carry three, nothing in the rows is high enough, and the only thing built to stand in the sea is the customs tower, three storeys above the old high-water, out toward the open sea.

Tam settled in the middle of the floating door. Jocosa refused Isk's nine coin, saying Isk's mother once lent her eleven and never asked for it back, and poled the door out into the flooded rows toward the customs tower through the rain.

Isk called out the floating wreckage while Jocosa poled the door through the flooded rows [[L9]] and across open swells to the customs tower. On its sheltered landward side an iron ladder runs from the waterline to the first window; Jocosa hooked a rung and held the door there.

Isk rested on the door under the customs tower [[L10]]'s ladder with her arm through a rung while Jocosa grudgingly held the door steady with the pole; Tam fell asleep. The storm beat on the seaward side. Isk got a little of her strength back.

Isk, Tam and Jocosa waited an hour in the lee of the customs tower [[L10]] as the storm blew out. Jocosa said Isk's mother always said the sea would come back and people laughed. The water stopped rising but has not gone down. Isk has some strength back.

Isk slept two hours on the floating door under the customs tower [[L10]]'s ladder, curled against Tam; the storm came back while they slept. Jocosa kept watch and held the door; nothing passed but timber and a drowned sheep, and the water held level. Isk woke stiff and hurt but with strength back.

Isk climbed the iron ladder into the customs tower [[L10]] through the first window; Jocosa called after her curtly not to fall. Inside is a dry square room with rotting customs ledgers and a spiral stair; fresh footprints, small and large, lead up the stair, and something metal ticks above.

Tam climbed into the tower after Isk. Up the spiral stair, the second floor had been lived in: a door-and-barrel table, a lantern, a sacking bed, and a ticking brass tide machine with channel names in Isk's mother's handwriting, over years of tide figures in the same hand. Fresh prints of a big boot and a small bare runner's foot led up.

Isk read the newest page: years of tide figures with a column headed 'bar' widening day by day, and under today's date a fresh note in her mother's hand: the sea crossed the outer bar three hours early, H. Jocosa Kettle says the reeve will move the mark and say nothing, and the bell must be rung, by her if not him. Tam sulked and wanted to go home. A light bare step sounded on the boards above.

At the top of the customs tower [[L10]], in the roofless bell-chamber, the customs bell lies on its side on rollers beside an empty oak frame. A thin, barefoot, grey-haired woman in a patched runner's oilskin, with Isk's jaw, stood beside it with a mallet and wedge and lowered them without a word. Tam called up the stair asking who it was.

The woman at the bell is Isk's mother, Mara Tarrow, alive. At Isk's voice she dropped her mallet and wedge, touched the reckoner at Isk's belt, and held her without a word. Tam, below on the stair, asked in disbelief whether she is real, since everyone knows she is on the red lamp.

Asked why she never came home, Mara could not speak, only rasp; she pointed at the sea, at the bell, at Isk, and pressed her hand to her chest. Tam, at the stair-head, said sharply not to ask him, then realised Mara cannot talk.

Mara wrote on a beam with charcoal: the reeve paid her to watch the sea in secret; H. came monthly, took her figures and brought food; she told them the sea was coming and the reeve promised to warn the town but never did. She pointed at the fallen bell and mimed ringing it. Tam guessed H. Una Rendle [[D]] is Hereward Jessop, the tide clerk, seen going out at dry tide with a basket.

Tam explained how to raise the fallen customs bell: rope over the iron hook on the frame's top beam, down to the bell's crown, and back to a stone mooring bollard turned like a capstan, wedging every turn. Mara brought two coils of old salt-stiff line and an iron bar. A new line of white is gathering on the bar toward evening.

Isk climbed the bell frame, passed the tarred rope through the iron hook, tied it to the bell's crown and ran the free end to the stone bollard. Tam scornfully said her knot would slip under the weight and to use two turns; Mara silently agreed.

Isk retied the bell knot with two turns as Tam said and set it hard. Tam, won over, told her his uncle said a knot is the only honest thing on a cart, and hopped over to the bollard to haul with her while Mara readied the wedges.

Isk and Tam turned the stone bollard while Mara wedged it; after eight turns the bell swung free a hand above the floor. Tam then turned on Isk: ringing it in the tower means no thirty coin for the bell he signed for first and lost his uncle's cart chasing, and he refused to turn the bar any further.

Isk told Tam that if the bell isn't rung there will be no town to sell it to, and gave him her purse of nine coins toward a new cart, promising to tell Una and his aunt he signed first. Tam took it, still sharp and afraid for his aunt on the low wall, and went back to the bar; the bell began to rise again.

Turning and wedging the bollard, Isk, Tam and Mara raised the bell; Isk climbed the frame and guided its rusted bearings into the sockets, and the customs bell hung in its frame again. Tam sat down exhausted and told her not to talk to him, just ring it.

Isk rang the rehung customs bell from the tower until her arms gave out; the sound carried over the new sea, and Saltmarrow [[L1]]'s temple bell answered faint and frantic across the water, followed by lanterns moving along the harbour wall. The town has been warned.

Isk, Mara and Tam slept in the bell-chamber. In the night Isk woke to see the Lantern Wives' lamps lit on poles and chimneys across the drowned rows; Mara stroked her hair as when she was small. At dawn of day two Isk woke stiff and aching but with her strength back; the sea has not gone down.

Isk used Tidecount at dawn: the sea is here to stay, but it now breathes like a true tide, twice a day; around midday it will fall far enough to bare the higher rows' roofs by a man's height and Saltmarrow's old mooring rings for an hour or two. Tam noticed her 'jaw thing' and asked what it says.

Tam realised Saltmarrow's wall is a harbour again. Asked to come home, Mara hesitated, looking at her machine and figures. Then Tam spotted a harbour skiff rowing out from Saltmarrow straight for the tower, two rowers and a thin man in a clerk's coat with a slate standing in the stern; Mara went white.

Hereward Jessop [[B]] arrived in a harbour skiff with two rowers. He said the reeve sent him to take the bell down before the guild saw it hung and bring Mara in quietly as a 'madwoman'; instead he dropped his slate in the sea, said he was done chalking the reeve's lies, apologised to Mara, and asked to take her home.

From the boat Hereward said flatly that Mara would never leave her tide clock, as she refused him every month. Mara went up, wrapped the brass machine in sacking and took all her papers, came down, wrote TOWN on the window sill in charcoal for Hereward to see, and climbed out onto the ladder to go.

Isk, Tam and Mara climbed down into the skiff and Hereward had the rowers take them home. They crossed the drowned rows to Saltmarrow, whose harbour wall now stands in the sea, crowded with townsfolk who shouted at the sight of the boat. The skiff came in to the bottom of the harbour stairs.

Isk helped Tam up the harbour stairs, with Mara and Hereward following, into a great crowd on the wall that began to say Mara's name. Philippa ran out of the chandlery and seized Tam, who apologised for losing his uncle's cart. Wulfstan [[C]] told Isk the town heard the bell while the reeve's men told them to go home, and asked if it was her.

Isk told the crowd on the wall that Mara had spent six years in the customs tower [[L10]] measuring the sea for the reeve, who knew and told no one. The crowd mostly doubted her, calling it grief; a woman said Mara drowned. Wulfstan [[C]], unconvinced, warned her the reeve's men in grey were coming down the wall and that she had no proof but a mute woman and a boy.

Hereward Jessop [[B]] stood on the bench by the tally board and confessed to the crowd: Mara is alive; the reeve found her on the outer bar six years ago and paid her to watch the sea from the customs tower [[L10]]; Hereward carried her figures monthly; the reeve locked them away, had the false tides chalked, and was told yesterday at first light but chose to wait to protect the guild's runners and his taxes. The crowd closed against the reeve's men.

Mara gave Isk her papers, and Isk pinned six years of tide figures over the guild contracts on the tally board. The crowd read them aloud to each other, Hereward pointed out pages, and Wulfstan [[C]] held up yesterday's sheet and said it was written down well enough for him. The crowd turned against the reeve.

Isk stood her ground at the tally board with Mara as four of the reeve's men in grey shoved through the hostile crowd; in the crush she was rammed against the board's frame and hurt her ribs again. Wulfstan [[C]] stepped up beside her and dared the men to take the figures down in front of everyone; Hereward stood on her other side. The leading man did not reach for anything.

The reeve's man left without a word to fetch him. Hereward said the reeve would come smiling. Reeve Baldwin Thorne arrived with his four men in grey, did not look at the figures, and greeted Mara warmly, telling her she should be resting.

Reeve Thorne took the page Isk held out, tore it up and threw it into the sea without reading it. Hereward told the crowd what it said, the sea over the outer bar three hours early and the reeve told by breakfast, and dared him to tear up six years of pages. Thorne called him overwrought; Wulfstan [[C]] dared him to read the next page, and Thorne did not move.

Thorne tried to dismiss Mara as mad and lead her home, but Mara stepped round him and wrote on the tally board: she knew the day, wrote it down, he read it and said wait; her name is Mara Tarrow, she is not mad, she was right. The woman who had doubted her covered her mouth, and the whole harbour took up the runners' whistle against Thorne.

Cornered, Reeve Thorne conceded in front of the town that Hereward may chalk the tides and Mara post her figures beside them, but warned Isk she must answer to the salvage guild for the customs bell she signed for, and that the guild remembers debts. He left with his men trailing at a distance.

At the tally-house window Isk surrendered the customs-bell contract, saying the bell is rung and stays in its tower. Una Rendle [[D]] lined out Isk's name with the note 'contract surrendered, bell rung for the town', and beside Tam's name wrote 'signed first' and showed it to him.

Una Rendle [[D]] told Isk her winter credit is fourteen coin at the guild rate, due at the new moon, and that surrendering the contract or ringing the bell does not clear it. Mara's lost share went into the guild's lost-runners' fund six years ago; Una said Mara must claim it from the guild masters herself. She half-closed the shutter.

Una told Isk to go and sit down. At the chandlery Philippa was bandaging Tam's shin while he ate by the stove, and Mara sat wrapped in a blanket with a cup. Philippa wordlessly gave Isk a bowl of hot food and pointed her to the bench beside Mara.

Isk went back into the chandlery and ate Philippa's stew beside Mara, who looked at Isk's rope-burnt hand. Philippa, still angry, said Tam nearly drowned for a bell never meant for the guild and that Mara let the town think her dead for six years; Tam warned her off, and she turned back to the stove, shaking.

Philippa softened, said she lit a Lantern Wives' lamp for Mara herself the first winter, and offered Isk and Mara a bed upstairs. She offered Isk fifteen coin to bring up her late husband Wat's hand cart whole from the fish market hole at midday low water.

Philippa agreed to the deal: Isk should go at midday low water in Hereward Jessop's skiff, still tied at the stairs. She lent Isk a coil of new hemp line and a pair of iron cart-hooks on a strap, to be returned with the cart, and asked her to come back safe.

Isk rested at the chandlery through the morning while Mara watched the brass reckoner and marked the tide on her hand. A woman in a fish-scaled apron told Philippa the guild masters have been shut in the guildhall since the bell, the reeve's shutters are up, and two of his men left inland at dawn with a laden mule. Near midday Mara signalled low water was close.

Hereward Jessop, waiting at the foot of the harbour stairs, eagerly agreed and rowed Isk out himself at low water. The sea had fallen as Mara said, baring the mooring rings and the rows' upper storeys. They reached the old fish market [[L7]], its doorway half under water, Tam's rope floating inside, and drifted in against the eaves.

Isk climbed into the old fish market [[L7]] through the roof onto the stone counter. In the drained-down hole lay Wat's hand cart on its side, whole. Hereward brought the skiff to the doorway and offered to pull from the boat while Isk hooked the cart.

Hereward brought the skiff inside the fish market. Isk climbed down into the cellar hole beside Wat's cart, but the iron hooks slid off the slimy axle twice and would not hold. The water in the cellar has begun to rise again.

Isk tied the new line under the cart's bed and through the wheel with Tam's two-turn knot and pushed while Hereward hauled from the skiff; the cart came up out of the hole onto the market floor, whole, with a W carved on its side. Hereward tied it to the skiff to tow home on the rising tide.

Isk and Hereward rowed out of the fish market and back to Saltmarrow [[L1]] on the incoming tide, towing Wat's cart behind on the line. Tam was waiting at the bottom of the harbour stairs, staring at the cart.

Isk and Hereward tried to haul the waterlogged cart up the harbour stairs; on the fifth stair Isk's bad knee gave, and the cart rolled back down to the bottom stair, unbroken. Wulfstan [[C]] called down to let it drain on its side for an hour and to get more hands from the watchers on the wall.

Isk and Tam tipped the cart on its side to drain. Hereward answered Isk's call for help, saying half the wall owes Wat Kemp, and went into the crowd recruiting hands; a cooper, two runners and Wulfstan [[C]] began to come down.

With the town's hands the drained cart went up the harbour stairs and along the wall to the chandlery. Philippa touched the carved W, took back her line and cart-hooks, and paid Isk fifteen coins in oilcloth. Hereward brushed off thanks, saying the town did it, and went to chalk proper tides.

Isk paid Una fourteen coins at the tally-house window and Una lined out her winter credit as settled. Una quietly said the guildhall has been talking since the bell about Mara's share in the lost-runners' fund and about paying a tide-reader now there is a sea, and that Isk's name came up favourably.

Isk fell asleep on the tally-house porch bench and slept through to dawn of day three. In the night the town sang and argued on the wall; a thief tried her purse in the dark and fled without it. By dawn the wind had turned cold from the east, the tide was out, and someone, Philippa, had put a blanket over her.

Isk walked the quiet morning wall past the tally board, where Hereward had chalked true low waters beside Mara's figures, to the chandlery. Philippa said Mara and Jocosa Kettle [[F]] are on the bottom stair at low tide, and Jocosa has come with her door to take down the red cloth from the Lantern Wives' lamp; Mara agreed.

Isk joined Mara and Jocosa on the bottom stair. Hereward called down curtly from the wall that low water lasts an hour and a quarter. The three poled out on Jocosa's door to the two roofs and held it beneath Nearby street with its faded red cloth.

At the Lantern Wives' lamp Isk held the door against the gable while Mara untied the six-year-old red cloth. Mara folded it and gave it to Jocosa, who said she had lit the lamp every long ebb for six years. Mara opened the lantern, showed its candle stub, and put a flint and steel in Isk's hand.

Isk struck flint and steel and lit the candle in the Lantern Wives' lamp, for nobody lost. Mara closed the lantern gently; Jocosa held the folded red cloth and wept silently. Hereward waved both arms from the distant harbour wall, and the tide turned under the door.

Una said the guild masters wrote Mara back among the living and returned her six years' share from the lost-runners' fund. The guild and town jointly offer a new post, tide-reader of the customs tower [[L10]]: keep the tower and bell, ring high and low water, post the figures daily, for four coin a week and the tower to live in, for Mara and Isk together.

Mara and Isk signed together under TIDE-READER, CUSTOMS TOWER in Una's ledger. Una blotted their names, called them tide-readers written in, the first new line in six years that is not a debt or a death, and told them to ring the high water tonight, four coin every seventh day, the tower theirs. Hereward raised his chalk to them.

At the chandlery Philippa was brusque and would not look up, telling Isk to go. Tam gave Isk back her purse of nine coins since he got the cart back, and said he would come out to the tower at the next low water to teach them knots. Philippa blew her nose loudly.

Una leaned out of the tally window and told them high water is at half six tonight and she expects to hear the bell by seven. Hereward rowed Isk and Mara out on the incoming tide past the drowned rows and the burnt-down lamp to the customs tower [[L10]], and hooked the ladder.

In the bell-chamber Isk used Tidecount: the tide fills all day to a big spring high water a little before half six this evening, nearly to the top of the harbour stairs. Mara shook her head and pointed at her beam figure, 18.20, ten minutes earlier, and would not be argued with.

Isk and Mara spent the day in the tower: Mara taught Isk her brass machine and the bar column, Isk showed her Tidecount, and they ate Philippa's bread. A scavenger boy in a washtub climbed the ladder and tried Isk's purse while she dozed; Mara chased him off with the mallet. By evening the spring tide stood high up the tower and nearly slack.

At 18.20 by the beam Isk and Mara rang the spring high water together, slow and steady, and the harbour wall answered with lantern after lantern. Then Mara spoke for the first time in six years: Isk's name.

Isk asked Mara to say her name again, too soon. Mara's voice caught; she pulled away angrily, backed against the bell frame with her hand at her throat, and wrote NOT YET on the beam in charcoal, snapping the stick, then stood with her back turned looking at the sea. Isk waited.

Isk wrote her first line on the beam under Mara's NOT YET: the date, high water 18.20, rung, answered, the first line in any hand but Mara's. Mara kept her back turned in hard silence at the seaward arch. The tide turned, Saltmarrow's lanterns went out as the town trusted the bell, and Mara's shoulders slightly eased.

rows.title: Drowned and town
rows.text: A drowned harbour town at the edge of mudflats the sea left behind.

rows.title: Wrong hours of Salvage debt and a tide
rows.text: Salvage, debt and a tide that keeps the wrong hours.

rows.title: The Leaving
rows.text: Forty years ago the sea drew back from Saltmarrow in one night and did not return; the lower harbour drowned in mud instead of water.

rows.title: Tide Greeting
rows.text: People greet each other with "Dry feet," and answer "And a long ebb," a wish that the flats stay walkable.

rows.title: The Lantern Wives
rows.text: A quiet circle of widows who keep lamps lit on the flats at night for runners who never came back; the guild calls them a nuisance, others leave them bread.

rows.label: Forest March
rows.description: Misty wood roads, small towns, low peaks.

rows.name: human
rows.traits: weathered and wind-burnt; live by the tide tables; patch everything twice
rows.ability_rules: good at holding breath and reading mud; salt in old wounds slows healing
